query: FCC high-entropy alloys lose substantial strength above 800 °C, motivating refractory high-entropy alloys. Equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW retains excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but has poor room-temperature ductility, and its irradiation resistance has been inferred computationally rather than established here experimentally. Studies of other refractory high-entropy alloys have found greater irradiation resistance than pure tungsten under helium implantation and self-healing behavior associated with enhanced atomic diffusion and redistribution. However, irradiation-induced amorphization, helium-energy-dependent blistering, and irradiation-enhanced precipitation have also been observed, indicating unresolved phase- and surface-stability risks. Given the need to preserve BCC structural stability and high-temperature mechanical performance while improving room-temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance, what intervention could achieve this balance? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted directional or quantitative outcomes relative to untreated NbMoTaW, the applicable temperature and irradiation boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor amount of boron (~0.1 at.%) to equal-atomic, single‐phase BCC NbMoTaW will promote the in situ formation of fine, intergranular boride precipitates that enhance grain boundary cohesion. This modification is expected to markedly improve room‐temperature ductility while preserving the excellent high‐temperature strength and BCC phase stability, and it may additionally mitigate irradiation‐induced damage through acting as sinks for He bubbles.
generation.material_initial_state: Equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW that exhibits excellent high-temperature strength (up to 1600 °C) but poor ductility at room temperature and has primarily been studied for its high-T mechanical properties with only inferred irradiation tolerance.
generation.intervention: Introduce a minor alloying addition (~0.1 at.%) of boron during alloy synthesis of NbMoTaW.
generation.conditions: Performance assessed at room temperature (where ductility improvements are required) and at high temperatures (up to ~1600 °C) as well as under irradiation conditions (e.g., He implantation at temperatures around 1023–1073 K with doses up to several dpa).
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a fine distribution of intergranular boride precipitates (akin to those reported in other RHEA systems) that reinforce grain boundary cohesion.
generation.mechanism: Boron promotes precipitation of borides at grain boundaries. These fine precipitates improve intergranular cohesion and suppress premature intergranular fracture, thereby enhancing room-temperature ductility. At the same time, the enriched interfaces may act as effective sinks for irradiation-induced He and defects, helping to mitigate bubble growth and hardening while the primary BCC matrix remains intact and maintains high-temperature mechanical performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to untreated NbMoTaW, the modified alloy should exhibit significantly increased ductility at room temperature (e.g., higher compressive or tensile plasticity), while still retaining high strength at elevated temperatures (up to 1600 °C) and showing reduced irradiation-induced hardening or defect accumulation.
generation.baseline: Untreated, equal-atomic BCC NbMoTaW, which is known for its excellent high-T strength and inferred irradiation resistance but suffers from poor ductility at ambient temperature.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected to hold from room temperature (improved ductility region) through high-temperature regimes (up to ~1600 °C) and under irradiation conditions representative of reactor environments (e.g., He implantation doses in the dpa range at ~1023–1073 K).
generation.uncertainty: The optimal boron concentration and the precise morphology, spatial distribution, and coherency of the boride precipitates are not fully established. There is also uncertainty as to whether the boride formation might adversely affect the BCC phase stability or if any detrimental secondary phase formation could occur at extreme conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of NbMoTaW alloy with ~0.1 at.% boron added and a control set without boron. Use consistent synthesis methods (e.g., via arc melting or additive manufacturing) to obtain single-phase BCC microstructures. Characterize the microstructure using TEM and atom probe tomography (APT) to confirm the presence, size, and distribution of intergranular boride precipitates. Perform room-temperature tensile or compressive tests to assess ductility, high-temperature mechanical tests (up to 1600 °C) to evaluate strength retention, and helium ion irradiation tests at temperatures around 1023–1073 K to measure irradiation-induced defect evolution (e.g., He bubble density/size and hardness changes).
measurements: Quantitative assessment of room-temperature ductility (tensile elongation or compressive plastic strain)
Microstructural analysis (TEM/APT) before and after irradiation
Nanoindentation hardness and irradiation-induced hardening data
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-added NbMoTaW alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in room-temperature ductility compared to the baseline, or if high-temperature strength degrades or irradiation-induced damage (e.g., He bubble formation or hardening) is more pronounced relative to the control, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In summary, careful microstructural examination of Al0.5NbTa0.8Ti1.5V0.2Zr was carried out in the present study using advanced TEM and APT techniques. The results reveal that the homogenized and slow cooled (~10 °C/min) microstructure (Condition (1)) has an ordered B2 phase as the continuous matrix, interspersed with discrete cuboidal-like pockets of a disordered BCC phase. While this microstructure morphologically resembles the γ (fcc) + γ’ (ordered L12) type microstructure observed in many Ni-base superalloys, it is “inverted” in the sense that the continuous matrix phase is the ordered B2 phase, resulting in limited compressive ductility. The ductility of this alloy was substantially increased via microstructural engineering involving controlled annealing treatments, resulting in a phase inversion. Consequently, the hard, ordered B2 compound that forms the continuous phase in Condition (1) is replaced by the more ductile, disordered, BCC phase in Condition (3). The resultant microstructurally-engineered RHEA not only exhibits high yield strength at room temperature (~1345 MPa) and 600 °C (~1423 MPa), but also substantial compressive ductility at room temperature (>20%). Boron has also been widely added in alloys to improve the cohesive strength of grain boundaries [], e.g., to change the fracture mode of Ni3Al from intergranular to transgranular and thus prevent early failure [], or to lower the migration rate of grain boundaries and inhibit grain growth at high temperatures []. Additionally, the short-range order in an Fe40Mn40Co10Cr10 alloy caused by the addition of boron atoms or the precipitation of borides was reported to retard the motion and increase the density of dislocations [], and the discontinuous intergranular precipitation of borides in high-strength steels avoided the intergranular fracture [], both improving the mechanical properties of the alloys [,]. As the grain-boundary brittleness is a major issue for BCC RHEAs, a minor amount of boron element (0.1 at.%) was hence added into an HfMoNbTaTiZr RHEA in the present study for potential precipitation of borides at the grain boundaries and improvement of grain boundary cohesion, then to yield a larger work hardenability and better ductility.
